claims.text: Overall tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the balance between mechanical passive-film disruption and electrochemical repassivation.
Changing the in situ electrochemical potential alters passive-film kinetics.
Potential-dependent passive-film kinetics control the coupling between wear and corrosion.
The proposed initial alloy possesses a stable, self-healing passive oxide film in the corrosive environment.
Controlled electrochemical potentials can enhance or suppress passive-film formation during sliding.
The protective surface film is cyclically removed and restored under wear-corrosion conditions.
Sliding mechanically disrupts the passive film.
After film disruption, the alloy repassivates through electrochemical processes.
Hindered repassivation leaves the protective film compromised.
A persistently compromised passive film increases both corrosion and mechanical wear.
Potentials promoting robust passive-film formation reduce total degradation.
Potentials that inhibit passive-film formation increase wear rate, corrosion rate, and total degradation relative to open circuit.
Potentials favoring rapid film reformation lower degradation relative to the open-circuit baseline.
Microstructural or phase-dependent mechanisms can become important enough that passive-film dynamics no longer govern degradation.
Alloy composition can significantly alter passive-film characteristics.
The degree to which passive-film kinetics control degradation may vary with alloy composition and environmental parameters.
A cathodic potential is expected to enhance passive-film formation, whereas an anodic potential is expected to hinder film reformation.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and surface microscopy can monitor passive-film thickness and continuity during the test.
